title: Vector Database Indexing Algorithms
description: Master Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) algorithms: HNSW, IVF-PQ, and choose the right index type for latency vs accuracy tradeoffs.

data.text: Exact nearest neighbor search requires computing distances to every vector in the database — computationally infeasible for large corpora. Approximate Nearest Neighbor algorithms trade perfect accuracy for dramatic speedups. The three dominant algorithms are HNSW (graph-based), IVF-PQ (quantization-based), and LSH (hash-based). Understanding their tradeoffs is essential for production RAG systems.

data.text: HNSW builds a multi-layer graph where top layers provide coarse-grained navigation and bottom layers provide fine-grained connectivity. During search, entry from the top layer navigates to increasingly dense layers until reaching the bottom. This produces near-optimal recall with O(log n) query complexity.

data.text: IVF-PQ: Inverted File with Product Quantization

IVF-PQ first partitions the vector space into Voronoi cells (coarse quantization), then compresses each vector into a compact binary/codebook representation (product quantization). At query time, only vectors in nearby cells are scanned, dramatically reducing computation. PQ can achieve 10-100x compression with moderate accuracy loss.

data.text: Index parameters need to be tuned per workload. EfSearch (HNSW) and Nprobe (IVF) can be adjusted at query time without rebuilding the index, enabling per-query optimization. For a production system, you can route high-priority queries (e.g., customer-facing search) with higher accuracy settings, and batch/recommendation queries with lower settings.

data.text: Rebuild the HNSW graph periodically as your data grows. A graph built on 10K vectors performs poorly at 1M vectors. Plan for re-indexing during low-traffic windows.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: HNSW offers the best speed-accuracy balance for datasets under ~100M vectors
IVF-PQ dramatically reduces memory usage at the cost of some accuracy, ideal for massive corpora
EfSearch/Nprobe parameters enable per-query accuracy tuning without reindexing
Higher M (HNSW) and Nlist (IVF) improve accuracy but increase build time and memory
Re-index periodically — graph quality degrades quadratically with dataset growth
data.takeaway: Select your ANN algorithm based on dataset size and accuracy requirements, then tune query-time parameters for per-query performance optimization.
